channel.title: Datapavan: News
channel.description: What has happened in this field, and what it means for someone with an Android phone.

item.title: Norway's record fine hits Microsoft's Xandr over Grindr users' advertising data
item.description: Norway's regulator fined ad firm Xandr, now Microsoft's, NOK 92 million for relaying Grindr users' data, which can reveal sexual orientation, through ad auctions without valid consent. Grindr's own NOK 65 million fine from 2021 was upheld on appeal in 2025. Opening an app can send your data to many ad companies at once, and the fact that you use an app can itself be sensitive.

item.title: Citizen Lab details Webloc, a tool that tracks phones through app and ad data
item.description: Citizen Lab reported that Webloc draws on data from consumer apps and digital advertising. Sales and contract documents claim up to 500 million devices and three years of history, which it could not check. Buyers it names include Hungarian intelligence and US agencies such as ICE. Location data that apps pass into advertising can end up in tools used by police and intelligence agencies.

item.title: Keenadu backdoor found in validly signed Android tablet firmware
item.description: Kaspersky found a backdoor built into firmware of Alldocube and other, unnamed tablets, in images with valid signatures and some over-the-air updates. It gives remote control and is mainly used for ad fraud. Kaspersky counted 13,715 users who met it or its modules. A valid signature did not mean the firmware was clean: the researchers think the code was added while it was being built.

item.title: Google disrupts IPIDEA, a proxy network built on ordinary apps
item.description: Google took legal action against IPIDEA and identified over 600 Android apps whose code connected to it, often through SDKs that paid developers per download. Their users' phones could carry strangers' traffic. Google says Play Protect on certified devices now warns about and removes apps known to use them. An app you chose for something else can lend your connection to others, and that traffic is tied to your address.

item.title: LANDFALL spyware targeted Samsung Galaxy phones through a flaw in image handling
item.description: Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 found Android spyware sent in malformed image files that used a Samsung flaw, patched in April 2025. Samples date from July 2024. Its code points to recording, location, photo and message theft. Delivery may have needed no tap; this is unconfirmed. The flaw was in Samsung's own image library, and the fix reached phones only through a security update.

item.title: Pixnapping: an Android app with no permissions could read other apps' screens
item.description: University researchers showed that a malicious app with no permissions can rebuild what other apps display, pixel by pixel, including two-factor codes, on Pixel 6 to 9 and Galaxy S25 phones. Google's September 2025 patch was bypassed, and a further fix was planned. It needs no permission, so a permission list would not reveal it. The researchers say they do not know if real attacks use it.

item.title: Study links VPN apps with over 700 million downloads into three families
item.description: Researchers tied Android VPN apps with over 700 million combined Google Play downloads into three families that look like separate companies. Some share hard-coded passwords that the paper says could let an attacker decrypt traffic. A VPN app sees all your traffic, and a store listing may not show who runs it or how well it protects you.

item.title: Stalkerware app Catwatchful exposes data from 26,000 victims' phones
item.description: A researcher found a flaw exposing about 62,000 customer logins of this hidden Android app, which takes photos, messages, location and live audio. TechCrunch reported phone data from about 26,000 victims and called it at least the fifth spyware operation with a data spill that year. These apps hide on the phone, and the private data they take can then leak from the seller's own servers.

item.title: Jury orders Google to pay $314.6 million over data Android phones sent while idle
item.description: A California jury found Google liable for Android phones exchanging data with it over users' cellular plans while idle, without permission, and awarded $314.6 million. A similar nationwide case, Taylor v. Google, reached a $135 million settlement in 2026. The case concerns data sent in the background on a plan the user pays for, not data the user chose to send.

item.title: FBI warns of BADBOX 2.0: millions of home devices infected, some before purchase
item.description: The FBI said millions of devices such as TV boxes and projectors joined the BADBOX 2.0 botnet through software set up before sale or apps required at setup. Google, which says the botnet infected over 10 million uncertified Android devices, sued the operators. Such software can be there before you unbox a device, and infected devices end up in proxy services that criminals use.

item.title: Facebook, Instagram and Yandex apps tied web browsing to users via a local channel
item.description: Researchers found Meta and Yandex scripts on websites passing identifiers to the companies' Android apps through the phone's own local ports, tying web visits to the user, even in Incognito mode. Both stopped after the disclosure in June 2025, the researchers say. No Android permission was needed, so nothing on the phone's permission screens showed this link.

item.title: WhatsApp warns about 90 people of Paragon spyware; traces found on Android phones
item.description: WhatsApp notified about 90 accounts it believed were targeted with Paragon's Graphite, including journalists and civil society members, after stopping an attack that needed no tap. Citizen Lab later reported signs of infection on Android phones in Italy. Citizen Lab notes Android's logs are sporadic, so finding no trace does not prove a phone was never infected.

item.title: Hack of Gravy Analytics shows how location data from apps reaches brokers
item.description: Hackers claimed to have stolen customer lists and smartphone location data from the broker Gravy Analytics, which later confirmed a breach. A lawsuit says the coordinates came through apps including Tinder, Grindr and Candy Crush. Location data from everyday apps can end up with companies the user has never heard of, and then with hackers.

item.title: A data broker's free sample held 3.6 billion location points from phones in Germany
item.description: Journalists at netzpolitik.org and Bayerischer Rundfunk got a free sample from broker Datastream with about 11 million device IDs over two months. They could trace individuals, including people who apparently work for ministries, the military and intelligence services. Location data from apps such as weather, navigation or dating apps can be bought, and movements can reveal who someone is.

item.title: Free VPN apps on Google Play secretly turned phones into proxies
item.description: HUMAN's researchers listed 28 Google Play apps, 17 of them free VPNs, that turned Android devices into proxy nodes through a monetisation SDK from LumiApps. Google removed all 28 and said Play Protect disables them. A free VPN can use your connection for other people's traffic, and the signs may be only slow internet or blocked sites.

item.title: FTC bars X-Mode from selling sensitive location data gathered through apps
item.description: An order proposed in January 2024 and finalised that April bars X-Mode (now Outlogic) from selling sensitive location data gathered through its SDK in other apps, its own apps and other brokers. The FTC reached similar orders with Gravy Analytics and, in a 2026 proposed settlement, Kochava. The FTC said an SDK inside ordinary apps fed this data, and that X-Mode did not reliably honour some Android users' opt-outs.

item.title: US senator says governments sought phone push-notification records
item.description: Senator Ron Wyden said his office was tipped off in 2022 that foreign government agencies were demanding push notification records from Apple and Google. The records show which app got a notification, when, and for which phone and account. He named no governments. Notifications pass through the phone system's provider, so records of which apps you use can exist outside your phone.

item.title: SpinOk SDK with spyware features found in apps with 421 million downloads
item.description: Doctor Web found a marketing SDK in 101 Google Play apps that could list and upload files and read or replace clipboard contents. It says a later version dropped these functions. BleepingComputer reports all but one of the ten most-downloaded listed apps were removed. Code a developer adds for advertising can reach your files and clipboard, and the app itself gives no sign of it.

item.title: Mozilla finds most top apps' Google Play safety labels false or misleading
item.description: Mozilla compared Data Safety labels with privacy policies for 40 top Google Play apps and found discrepancies in nearly 80%. It graded 16 apps Poor, 15 Needs Improvement and 6 OK; 3 did not fill in the form. Developers report the labels themselves. The label in the store is the developer's own declaration, and Google says apps are responsible for its accuracy.

item.title: Phone makers' platform signing keys were found signing Android malware
item.description: Google's Android security team listed ten malware samples signed with leaked platform keys, the keys that can give an app system-level access. Keys of Samsung, LG, Revoview and MediaTek were among those identified; the owners of some others were not. An app signed with such a key can ask for the same privileges as the system, with wide access to data on the phone.

item.title: Google removes apps carrying a data-collecting SDK estimated on 60 million devices
item.description: Researchers at AppCensus found an SDK from Panama's Measurement Systems in Google Play apps, taking phone numbers, email addresses and GPS data and able to read the clipboard. Apps with it were estimated on at least 60 million devices. Google removed dozens in March 2022. Ordinary apps, including prayer and speed-trap apps, carried this code, and its maker paid developers to include it.
